summary: This BCP gives IANA revised guidance for managing values in the fields of IGMP and MLD protocol headers. It sets how new values are assigned in these group management protocols. It obsoletes RFC 3228.

plainLanguage.summary: When many people want to add names to a shared list, someone needs rules. This tells the list keeper how to hand out new codes for multicast group protocols.

questions: how are igmp and mld values assigned
how are igmp type numbers assigned
what are the igmp mld query flags
subtitle: The rulebook IANA follows when handing out new values in the IGMP and MLD headers, replacing RFC 3228.

tldr.problem: IGMP (IPv4) and MLD (IPv6) headers carry Type, Code and Flags fields whose values must be assigned without collisions, but the old guidance in RFC 3228 covered only IGMP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9778 updates the IGMP registries to Standards Action, points MLD at the ICMPv6 registry, and creates two new flag registries shared by IGMP and MLD.
tldr.outcome: IPv4 and IPv6 group management protocols now share one set of allocation guidelines, and RFC 3228 is obsoleted.

today: RFC 9778 is a Best Current Practice published in March 2025 that obsoletes RFC 3228. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What This Document Does
sections.content:
RFC 9778 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 57) that gives IANA, the keeper of protocol number registries, allocation guidelines for fields in the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) and Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) headers. IGMP is defined in STD 100 and MLD in STD 101. Some of the registries it describes were created earlier, and others are created by this document.

The document obsoletes RFC 3228 and unifies the guidelines for the IPv4 and IPv6 group management protocols. It uses the registration procedures defined in RFC 8126.
sections.plainLanguage: Two groups of multicast helpers, one for each kind of Internet address, have codes in their messages. This paper tells the list keeper how to give out new codes for both groups the same way.

sections.title: IGMP Type and Code Registries
sections.content:
The IGMP header has two fields whose values come from IANA-managed name spaces: Type and Code. Code values are defined relative to a specific Type value.

RFC 3228 created the "IGMP Type Numbers" registry and the "Code" Fields registry. RFC 9778 updates both in the same way: the registration procedure changes to Standards Action, and the reference changes from RFC 3228 to this document.

The policy for assigning Code values under a brand new IGMP Type MUST be defined in the document that defines that Type.
sections.plainLanguage: To add a new kind of IGMP message, you now need a full official standard, not just a quick request. If the new message has sub-codes, its own paper must say how those are handed out.

sections.title: MLD Type and Code Fields
sections.content:
The MLD header also has Type and Code fields. RFC 9778 does not create a new registry for them. Their assignment is defined in RFC 4443 with a registration policy of IETF Review, and the values live in the ICMPv6 parameters registry at IANA.

So IGMP type values follow Standards Action, while MLD type values follow the IETF Review policy already set by the ICMPv6 specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The IPv6 helpers already have their code list somewhere else, and that list has its own rules. This paper just points to it.

sections.title: Query and Report Message Flags
sections.content:
IANA has created two registries for bits in the Flags field of the group management messages. Both apply to IGMP and MLD together.

  • "IGMP/MLD Query Message Flags" covers the Flags field of the IGMPv3 Query and the MLDv2 Query. Bit 0 is E (Extension), referencing RFC 9279. Bits 1 to 3 are unassigned.
  • "IGMP/MLD Report Message Flags" covers the Flags field of the IGMPv3 Report and the MLDv2 Report. Bit 0 is again E (Extension), referencing RFC 9279. Bits 1 to 15 are unassigned.

The Flags Bit value in each registry corresponds to the column header in the packet format diagrams of the IGMPv3 and MLDv2 specifications. Assigning a new bit flag in either registry requires Standards Action.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has a few tiny on/off switches. Only one switch, labeled E, has a job so far. If anyone wants to give another switch a job, they need an official standard.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Firewalls and intrusion detection monitors often rely on unambiguous interpretation of these header fields. When a new value is assigned, an analyzer that does not understand it may fail. If it declines to forward the unknown traffic, connectivity is lost. If it forwards the traffic and the new value is part of an attack, security is lost.

The RFC argues that this risk calls for high visibility for assignments, which the Standards Action process ensures.
sections.plainLanguage: Guards at the gate know the list of normal codes. If a strange new code shows up, they might wrongly block it or wrongly wave it through, so new codes should be announced loudly.

sections.title: What Changed From RFC 3228
sections.content:
RFC 3228 was written by Bill Fenner for IPv4 IGMP only, and it supplied a portion of the content of RFC 9778. The changes are:

  • The IGMP Type and Code registries move to Standards Action, with references pointing to RFC 9778.
  • MLD is brought into the same document, with its Type and Code assignment pointed at the ICMPv6 registry.
  • Two new shared flag registries are created for Query and Report messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule sheet only covered one of the two groups. The new one covers both and adds a list for the on/off switches.
